items.title: Nirvana is not heaven — it is the cessation of craving
items.claim: How does Buddhism understand nirvana (nibbana in Pali)?

options.text: The 'blowing out' of the fires of greed, hatred and delusion — the end of suffering and rebirth, attainable in this life as well as at death (parinirvana)
A meditative trance state achieved daily

items.reveal:
The Pali 'nibbana' / Sanskrit 'nirvana' literally means 'blowing out' — as a flame is extinguished. The image is from the Adittapariyaya Sutta (Fire Sermon).

Nirvana attained in life is sometimes distinguished from parinirvana — the full nirvana at death of an enlightened being. The Buddha attained nirvana under the Bodhi tree (around age 35) and parinirvana around age 80.

The Buddha refused to speculate about nirvana's metaphysical status — whether the enlightened being exists, doesn't exist, both or neither after death (Aggi-Vacchagotta Sutta). Speculation does not lead to liberation.
items.why: Translating nirvana as 'heaven' imports Christian assumptions. The Buddhist concept is structurally different — not a destination but an end, not a reward but a release.

items.title: Paley's watchmaker argument (1802) was anticipated by Hume's critique
items.claim: What is Paley's design argument and how did Hume respond?

options.text: Paley accepted Hume's criticism and abandoned the design argument

Paley's 'Natural Theology' (1802) argued from the complexity of a found watch to a designer, by analogy with biology. Hume's 'Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion' (1779, posthumous) had already attacked the analogy — universe is unlike a watch, the analogy points to an apprentice or committee of designers, not a single benevolent God
Hume defended a stronger version of the argument

items.reveal:
William Paley's 'Natural Theology' (1802) opens with the watch-on-the-heath analogy. He uses the human eye as his prime biological example.

Hume's 'Dialogues' (1779, published posthumously) anticipated and refuted versions of the design argument decades earlier. Three main lines: the universe is not closely analogous to a watch; the analogy could equally suggest a committee, apprentice or evil designer; the argument cannot reach a single benevolent God of classical theism.

Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species' (1859) provided a non-design explanation for biological complexity. Modern Intelligent Design (Behe, Dembski, 1990s onwards) is a controversial attempt to revive the argument scientifically.
items.why: The design argument keeps returning in new forms. Each version has to deal with the next development in science — biological evolution, cosmic fine-tuning, multiverse cosmology — making it a moving target rather than a settled debate.

items.title: Moral and natural evil are distinct problems for theism
items.claim: What is the distinction between moral and natural evil?

options.text: All evil is caused by human moral failure

Moral evil is caused by free moral agents (murder, torture, cruelty); natural evil is caused by impersonal natural processes (earthquakes, disease, predation) — they raise different problems for theistic theodicies
Natural evil is just a subset of moral evil

items.reveal:
Free Will Defence (Augustine, Alvin Plantinga) explains moral evil as the cost of human free will — but doesn't obviously address natural evil. Earthquakes do not flow from human choices.

Irenaean theodicy (revived by John Hick, 'Evil and the God of Love', 1966) sees natural evil as part of soul-making — character development requires a challenging environment.

Augustinian theodicy treats evil as privatio boni (privation of good) — not a substance but an absence. The Fall extends moral consequences into nature.

The logical problem of evil (J. L. Mackie, 'Evil and Omnipotence', 1955) has been largely answered by Plantinga's free-will defence; the evidential problem (William Rowe, 1979) remains live.
items.why: The problem of evil is the most persistent challenge to classical theism. The moral/natural and logical/evidential distinctions shape which theodicies are even relevant — generic answers miss the structure of the argument.
